subject: William Shakespeare
overview: William Shakespeare was a glover's son from the market town of Stratford-upon-Avon who went to London and became an actor, poet and the most performed playwright in the English language. Over roughly twenty-five years he wrote or co-wrote around 39 plays, including Hamlet, Macbeth, Romeo and Juliet and The Tempest, along with 154 sonnets, most of them staged by his own acting company at the Globe theatre on the south bank of the Thames. He spent his last years back in Stratford, a prosperous property owner, and died there in 1616.

key_moments.title: An 18-year-old marries in Stratford
key_moments.text: In late 1582 the young Shakespeare married **Anne Hathaway**, a woman about eight years older than him. Six months later their daughter **Susanna** was baptised, followed in 1585 by twins, **Hamnet and Judith**. Then the record goes quiet: for roughly seven years almost nothing is known of where Shakespeare was or what he did, a gap biographers call **the lost years**.
claims: William Shakespeare married Anne Hathaway in 1582, when he was 18.
Anne Hathaway was about eight years older than William Shakespeare.
Susanna, the daughter of William Shakespeare and Anne Hathaway, was baptised about six months after the wedding, in 1583.
The twins Hamnet and Judith Shakespeare were born in 1585, and little is recorded of William Shakespeare's life between 1585 and 1592, a period called the lost years.

key_moments.title: First sighting in London, as a target
key_moments.text: The first sign that Shakespeare had made it in the London theatre is an insult. A pamphlet published under the name of the dramatist **Robert Greene**, Greene's Groats-Worth of Wit, warned university-educated playwrights about an **"upstart Crow"** who thought himself "the only Shake-scene in a country". The jab borrowed and twisted a line from Shakespeare's own **Henry VI, Part 3**, so his earliest known review mocked him in his own words.
claims: Greene's Groats-Worth of Wit, published in 1592 under Robert Greene's name, attacked an "upstart Crow" generally taken to be William Shakespeare.
The Groats-Worth of Wit passage puns on Shakespeare's name with the phrase "Shake-scene".
The "upstart Crow" passage parodies a line from William Shakespeare's Henry VI, Part 3.

key_moments.title: A company, a theatre, a royal patron
key_moments.text: From 1594 Shakespeare wrote for, acted with and part-owned the **Lord Chamberlain's Men**, whose star actor was **Richard Burbage**. In a dispute over the lease of their Shoreditch playhouse, The Theatre, the company had its timbers dismantled and carried across the Thames to build the **Globe** in 1599. In 1603 the new king, **James I**, took the troupe under his own patronage and it became the **King's Men**. As a shareholder Shakespeare took a cut of the company's takings, not just a fee for his scripts, and he retired a wealthy man.
claims: William Shakespeare was a member and part-owner of the Lord Chamberlain's Men from 1594.
After a dispute over the lease of The Theatre in Shoreditch, the Lord Chamberlain's Men used its timbers to build the Globe Theatre in 1599.
After James I came to the throne in 1603, the Lord Chamberlain's Men became the King's Men.
Richard Burbage was the leading actor of William Shakespeare's company.

key_moments.title: The First Folio saves half the plays
key_moments.text: Seven years after Shakespeare's death, two fellow actors from the King's Men, **John Heminges and Henry Condell**, gathered 36 of his plays into one large volume, now called the **First Folio**. **Ben Jonson** wrote verses for it praising Shakespeare as "not of an age, but for all time". About half of those plays, including Macbeth, The Tempest and Twelfth Night, had never been printed before, so without the Folio they would very likely have been lost.
claims: The First Folio of William Shakespeare's plays was published in 1623.
John Heminges and Henry Condell compiled the First Folio.
The First Folio contains 36 plays, about 18 of which had not been printed before, including Macbeth, The Tempest and Twelfth Night.
Ben Jonson wrote in the First Folio that Shakespeare was "not of an age, but for all time".

deep_facts.text: Shakespeare's will leaves money, houses and land mostly to his daughter Susanna. His wife Anne is mentioned only once, in a line inserted between the existing lines: he leaves her his "second best bed with the furniture". Readers have taken it as a snub for centuries. Some historians argue the opposite, that the best bed was kept for guests and the second-best was the couple's own marriage bed, and that a widow was entitled to part of the estate by law anyway.
claims: William Shakespeare's will left most of his estate to his elder daughter Susanna.
William Shakespeare's will left his wife Anne his "second best bed", in a line inserted between the existing lines.
Some historians argue the second-best bed was the marital bed and that Anne Hathaway was entitled to a share of the estate by law.

deep_facts.text: Shakespeare lies under the chancel floor of Holy Trinity Church in Stratford, and the stone over him carries a verse instead of his name. It blesses whoever spares the stones and ends: "And cursed be he that moves my bones." The grave has never been opened, yet a radar survey in 2016 found signs of disturbance at the head end, which fits an old story that his skull was stolen.
claims: William Shakespeare is buried in the chancel of Holy Trinity Church in Stratford-upon-Avon.
William Shakespeare's gravestone carries an epitaph ending "And cursed be he that moves my bones."
A ground-penetrating radar survey of William Shakespeare's grave in 2016 suggested disturbance at the head end, consistent with a story that his skull had been taken.

deep_facts.text: Shakespeare and Miguel de Cervantes are both recorded as dying on 23 April 1616, and UNESCO picked 23 April as World Book Day partly for that reason. But the coincidence is an illusion created by the calendar. Spain had already moved to the Gregorian calendar, while England stayed on the older Julian one, which was ten days behind. The two writers actually died about ten days apart, and Cervantes went first.
claims: William Shakespeare's death date of 23 April 1616 is a Julian calendar date.
Spain used the Gregorian calendar in 1616 while England used the Julian calendar, which was ten days behind.
Miguel de Cervantes died in 1616, about ten days before William Shakespeare.
UNESCO chose 23 April for World Book Day in part because of the deaths of Shakespeare and Cervantes.
